title: Adani Eyes Overseas Airports, Joins Catania Bidders as $1 Billion Fundraise Closes
excerpt: The Financial Times reports the Adani Group is planning an international airports push; Reuters has reported the group is among the bidders for Sicily's Catania airport, as a $1 billion fundraise values Adani Airport Holdings at $18 billion.
body:
• The Financial Times reports that the Adani Group is planning an international airports push; Reuters has separately reported that the group is among the bidders for Sicily's Catania airport.
  • The move comes as a $1 billion fundraise values Adani Airport Holdings at about $18 billion, with Temasek, BlackRock, Alpha Wave and Premji Invest taking up to a 5.54% stake.
  • Adani runs eight Indian airports handling about a quarter of the country's passenger traffic, and has outlined $11 billion of domestic airport investment by 2030.
  • Analysts say going global could add to the bottom line and bring operating best practices back to India — though the group's overseas ventures have a chequered political history.

The overseas push

The Adani Group is planning an international airports push, the Financial Times reported this week, a move that would take India's largest airport operator beyond its home market for the first time. According to Reuters, the group is already among the bidders for Sicily's Catania airport — its first serious attempt at running an airport outside India.

The reported push reverses a pause: as recently as late 2025, the group had signalled it was concentrating on India, with Jeet Adani, a director at Adani Airport Holdings, saying the domestic business would expand three to four times over five to six years.

Why now: the $1 billion war chest

The international move follows a blockbuster fundraise. Adani Enterprises announced on Wednesday that it had agreed to sell up to a 5.54% stake in Adani Airport Holdings, raising about $1 billion from a consortium of Temasek, BlackRock, Alpha Wave and Premji Invest, valuing the airport operator at roughly $18 billion before the investment. Adani Enterprises remains the controlling shareholder.

The funds are earmarked for expanding and modernising the airport network, developing airport-linked commercial infrastructure and scaling adjacent businesses such as ground handling and passenger services — capital that could equally underwrite overseas bids. Adani CFO Jugeshinder Singh had told the Economic Times in June 2025 that the airports unit might raise around $1 billion from international investors as it evaluated growth plans and acquisitions.

The domestic engine

Adani entered the airport business only in 2019, winning contracts to operate six Airports Authority of India airports before acquiring the GVK group's stake in Mumbai, India's second-busiest airport. It now runs eight airports — Ahmedabad, Lucknow, Mangaluru, Mumbai, Jaipur, Guwahati, Thiruvananthapuram and the newly operationalised Navi Mumbai — handling nearly 25% of India's passenger traffic and a third of its air cargo.

The financials have strengthened alongside the expansion. Revenue from operations rose 34.4% in fiscal 2026, while profit after tax more than doubled to ₹1,731 crore, according to Outlook Business. The company has drawn up a ₹40,000 crore capital expenditure plan for fiscal 2027, with airports accounting for nearly ₹17,000 crore.

It has also been lobbying New Delhi to open up international flying rights, urging bilateral capacity expansions with the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Singapore, Indonesia and Malaysia — arguing it was a "criminal waste of assets" being built by airport operators to cap the flights serving them.

"It is the right strategy for an Indian airport company like Adani to look beyond India. Entering global markets not just adds to the bottom line but also helps learn best practices available elsewhere that can be used in India."

— Mark D. Martin, chief executive, Martin Consulting

What the international move means

Analysts have long argued that an overseas airport portfolio would be a natural extension of Adani's hard-asset model. Jeet Adani told Reuters in December that the group's "comfort and our core competency is in creating hard assets on the ground, long-gestation assets, running them quite efficiently" — a description that fits airports anywhere.

But overseas ventures carry political risk, and Adani has felt it. After US prosecutors indicted top group officials in November 2024, Kenya rescinded a Nairobi airport renovation contract, a reminder that airport deals abroad can become geopolitical lightning rods. Reuters Breakingviews recently cautioned that Adani's growing overseas ambitions, while aligned with the conglomerate's broader strategy, "appear opportunistic and harder to realise" than its India opportunities.

What's next

The Catania bid will be the first real test of whether the Financial Times' reported push translates into deals. At home, the group says it will bid aggressively for all 11 airports the Indian government plans to lease to private operators, including Amritsar and Varanasi, and has signalled an initial public offering or demerger of the airports unit once the business turns cash positive. For investors, the $18 billion valuation puts a public-market marker on what was, seven years ago, a startup airport operator — and an international push would test how far that model travels.
image_caption: Adani Group chairman Gautam Adani. Adani Airports is bidding for overseas airports as it builds a $1 billion fund.
nri_angle: For diaspora investors and travellers, a global Adani airports network would put an Indian operator on the flight paths many NRIs travel.
